procedure.title: Get an import certificate from Japan's Narcotics Control Department
procedure.authority: Narcotics Control Department (NCD), Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare
procedure.leadTime: Apply at least 14 days before you travel. NCD says its Tokyo office can't accept last-minute applications for any reason.
documents: The import application form from the NCD page. There are separate forms for narcotics and for stimulants' raw materials.
The export application form as well, if you'll leave Japan with leftover medicine. If you won't, say in your email that you don't need an export permit.

A medical certificate from the doctor who prescribed the medicine, issued within the last 3 months. It must give your name and current address, the specific reason you take the medicine, each medicine with its dose and strength, and the doctor's signature. NCD doesn't accept a reason like "for personal use" or "for travel".
Photos of your own medicine packages, showing the name and strength, as JPEG, PDF or Word files. NCD can't open HEIC photos.

Arriving at Haneda or Narita: also a driver's licence or utility bill confirming your address (not needed if the address is on the medical certificate). If you'll stay more than 90 days, also your visa, work contract or letter of acceptance.
steps: Check your medicine's category on NCD's controlled substances list. This permit is for narcotics and stimulants' raw materials. Amphetamine (Adderall) and methamphetamine can't be brought in at all.

Fill in the import form, and the export form if you're taking leftovers home. Give your arrival date as the time of entry. For the reason for departure, write "To return home" or "To go to another country", not "For vacation".
Get the medical certificate from your prescribing doctor and photograph your medicine packages.

Send everything by email, fax or post to the NCD office that covers your arrival airport. If your files are over 10 MB, split them across several emails, then send a short follow-up asking NCD to confirm it received them.
Travel with the medicine and the import certificate NCD sends you.
procedure.atTheBorder: Show the import certificate to the customs officer. You must carry the medicine yourself: it can't be posted to Japan or carried for you by someone else, even family.

Items without a government-issued inspection certificate from the exporting country can't be brought in, even as souvenirs or for personal consumption, and it says such certificates are generally hard to get for personal-use products, so most animal products can't be brought in. This applies whether the products are for yourself, gifts, bought in a shop (including at an airport), home-made, heat-processed or vacuum-packed. Dairy products carried in passenger baggage are excluded from its list of products subject to animal quarantine. Violators can be arrested and are punishable with imprisonment or a fine; since 1 July 2020 the maximum fine has been ¥3 million.

notes: The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 defines "cannabis (hemp)" to cover charas (resin/hashish/hash oil) and ganja (the flowering or fruiting tops) — both are prohibited narcotic drugs, and importing them into India carries severe criminal penalties. The statutory definition of cannabis excludes seeds and leaves when not accompanied by the flowering/fruiting tops (the basis for bhang, a leaf-based preparation, being treated differently under Indian law domestically) — but this carve-out is about domestic cultivation/sale, not a confirmed customs import allowance, and no primary CBIC/NDPS source describing a personal-import allowance for CBD oil or hemp-derived products (with or without a foreign prescription) was found in this pass. Whether CBD oil or hemp-derived products can be brought in isn't answered by any official page read; ask Indian Customs (CBIC) before travelling with them.

limits.description: The Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act, 2019 makes it a criminal offence for any person to produce, manufacture, import, export, transport, sell, distribute, or advertise electronic cigarettes (or any part of one) in India — there is no personal-use or personal-baggage exemption in the Act's text.

notes: Section 7 penalty for a first offence: up to 1 year imprisonment and/or a fine up to Rs. 1,00,000 (one lakh); a second or subsequent offence carries up to 3 years imprisonment and a fine up to Rs. 5,00,000 (five lakh). This is a genuine, high-stakes traveler trap: a device that is legal and commonly carried in many other countries is a criminal offence to bring into India, not merely a confiscated item.
summary: Banned: India's 2019 Act makes importing e-cigarettes a criminal offence, with no personal-use exemption.

limits.description: Import of drones (Unmanned Aircraft Systems) in Completely-Built-Up (CBU), Semi-Knocked-Down (SKD), or Completely-Knocked-Down (CKD) form is classified "Prohibited" under India's ITC (HS) 2022 import policy (Chapter 88, Policy Condition No. 03, as revised by DGFT Notification No. 54/2015-20 dated 9 Feb 2022). The only stated exceptions are: (i) government entities, government-recognised educational/R&D institutions, and drone manufacturers importing for R&D, each requiring a DGFT import authorisation; and (ii) drones for defence and security purposes, also requiring DGFT authorisation. Import of drone components (not assembled units) is classified "Free".

notes: No exception for tourists or personal/recreational use is stated anywhere in this notification — a foreign visitor's personal camera drone falls squarely within the prohibited CBU category, with no realistic path to a DGFT import authorisation. This is a genuinely high-risk item: many travelers assume a personal drone is fine to pack, and India's rule is stricter than most destinations already in this dataset.
summary: Prohibited: India bans drone imports, except by government, R&D bodies and manufacturers with a DGFT authorisation.

legal_source.name: Australian Border Force — Duty free

limits.description: 25 cigarettes or 25 grams of tobacco in any form duty-free per traveller aged 18 or over; no concession for travellers under 18. Most tobacco products (cigarettes, molasses tobacco, heat-not-burn, loose-leaf) are otherwise classed as prohibited imports beyond the personal concession.

notes: No permit is needed to bring tobacco products as a traveller within the concession. Exceeding the limit means duty/tax applies to all tobacco carried, not just the excess.
summary: Duty-free from age 18: 25 cigarettes or 25 g of tobacco. Go over it and duty applies to all the tobacco you carry, not just the excess.

legal_source.name: Australian Border Force — Duty free

limits.description: Since 24 July 2026 you can't bring nicotine pouches into Australia. The traveller's exemption no longer covers them, and a prescription doesn't help: personal importation is closed too. The Australian Border Force seizes them. Pouches could only be imported lawfully if they were on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods, and as at 24 July 2026 none were.

notes: This is separate from Australia's rules for tobacco (a 25-cigarette or 25 g allowance) and vapes (a small traveller's exemption). Import offences under the Therapeutic Goods Act can carry up to 5 years' imprisonment, a large fine, or both, depending on the circumstances.
summary: Banned since 24 July 2026: nicotine pouches can't be brought in, even with a prescription. The Australian Border Force seizes them.

legal_source.name: Australian Border Force — Australian Customs Notice No. 2026/29, Changes to nicotine pouch regulations (22 July 2026)

limits.description: Must declare if carrying AUD 10,000 or more (or foreign-currency equivalent), combined across cash and non-cash monetary instruments (bearer negotiable instruments), when entering or leaving Australia. No limit on the amount that may be carried — only a duty to declare at or above the threshold.

notes: Applies to citizens, residents, and visitors alike, in both directions. Splitting cash among travellers to stay under the threshold ("structuring") is a criminal offence. Money transferred via a bank or remittance provider does not need to be declared.

legal_source.name: AUSTRAC — Moving money overseas

limits.description: Traveller's exemption: up to a 3-month supply of most personal medicines (including some controlled substances) for the traveller or an immediate family member travelling with them, without needing special permission

notes: Keep medicine in original packaging with dispensing labels; carry the prescription or a doctor's letter stating what you're taking and how much. Cannot bring medicines for anyone else or sell/supply them. Some medicines require a permit or prescription and others cannot be brought at all — check the TGA/Office of Drug Control before travelling for anything unusual.

legal_source.name: Therapeutic Goods Administration — Entering Australia (travelling with medicines and medical devices)

notes: Cannabis and cannabis-containing therapeutic goods are excluded from the general personal-importation scheme and are prohibited imports under the Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956, EXCEPT under the traveller's exemption: a traveller may import medicinal cannabis for their own medical treatment (or that of someone they're caring for) if it was prescribed by a medical practitioner and supplied through a pharmacy, up to a 3-month supply per the prescription (or, for medicinal cannabis vapes, without the 3-month cap under a separate exemption). Recreational/non-prescribed cannabis is prohibited outright, with no CBD-specific carve-out confirmed for travellers. Evidence (prescription/label) may be required on entry.
summary: Only prescribed medicinal cannabis, supplied through a pharmacy, up to 3 months' supply under the traveller's exemption. Anything else is a prohibited import.

legal_source.name: Therapeutic Goods Administration — Medicinal cannabis: importation and the traveller's exemption

limits.description: Traveller's exemption for vapes entering by ship or aircraft, for the traveller's own use (or someone they're caring for who is travelling with them): maximum 2 vapes, 20 vape accessories (cartridges/capsules/pods), and 200 mL of vape substance in liquid form

notes: Vapes cannot otherwise be purchased from overseas retailers or websites and mailed/couriered into Australia for personal use, even with a prescription — that route is prohibited outright. Vapes containing controlled drugs (e.g. cannabis) are not covered by these quantity limits and are treated as prohibited drugs instead. Significant penalties apply for unlawfully importing vaping goods.
summary: Traveller's exemption, by air or sea, for your own use: up to 2 vapes, 20 accessories (pods, cartridges) and 200 ml of vape liquid.

legal_source.name: Therapeutic Goods Administration — Vapes: information for individuals and patients

notes: Strict, product-specific biosecurity import conditions apply and can change quickly with disease outbreaks (check BICON before travelling). Broadly: canned/retorted meat is permitted if commercially manufactured, shelf-stable, and (except canned poultry) labelled as made in a country free from foot-and-mouth disease. Uncanned/fresh meat, ham, bacon, salami and sausages from any country other than New Zealand are NOT allowed without an import permit; New Zealand-sourced uncanned meat (excluding pork and poultry) is allowed if declared and correctly labelled. Pork-derived jerky/biltong is never permitted for personal use; non-pork jerky is allowed up to 1 kg under specific labelling/packaging conditions. Cheese, butter and other dairy products are permitted for personal use up to 10 kg/10 litres if commercially packaged and made in a foot-and-mouth-disease-free country; must be declared and inspected on arrival. Non-compliant goods are exported or destroyed at the traveller's expense.

legal_source.name: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Bringing or mailing goods to Australia

notes: Official traveller advice: "do not carry any fresh fruit or vegetables, plants, seeds, meat and animal or wood products" into Australia — for faster border clearance, travellers are told simply not to bring these. Most live plants require a Department-issued import permit; seeds must be a permitted species, phytosanitary-certified, and free of contamination, or they will be exported/destroyed. Declare any risk goods on arrival or dispose of them in terminal bins. Providing false/misleading declarations or failing to comply with a biosecurity officer's directions can draw an infringement notice of up to AUD 6,600, civil penalty proceedings, or criminal prosecution, and can lead to visa cancellation and a re-entry ban of up to 3 years.

legal_source.name: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Travelling to Australia

notes: The Department of Home Affairs grants permission to import certain firearms and firearm-related articles under Schedule 6 to the Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; apply through its Firearms Portal. The portal notes 2026 firearms reforms (Combatting Antisemitism, Hate and Extremism Bill (Firearms and Customs Laws) 2026) being implemented with state and territory Firearms Registries.

legal_source.name: Dubai Customs — Declaring Money Procedure / Passenger Customs Guide, Version 6 (2025)

The report can be filed online (within 72 hours of travel) or on the paper NZCS 337 form at the border. There is no cap on how much cash may be carried — this is a reporting obligation, not a fee — but failing to declare is a criminal offence that can lead to fines, imprisonment, and seizure of the cash.

legal_source.name: New Zealand Customs Service — Border Cash Report

limits.description: Cash declaration thresholds for travelers entering mainland China
limits.quantity: RMB (CNY) cash: capped at 20,000 yuan per person per entry/exit — amounts above must be declared to Customs and undeclared excess can be turned back/confiscated. Foreign currency cash: no fixed maximum amount for bringing it INTO China, but any amount exceeding the equivalent of USD 5,000 must be declared in writing to Customs on arrival.

notes: The written-declaration trigger derives from the (国家外汇管理局/海关总署) Interim Measures for the Administration of Carrying Foreign Currency Cash Into and Out of the Country, read together with the Measures of the Customs of the PRC on the Supervision of Inbound and Outbound Passenger Baggage and Articles (effective 1 April 2025), whose Article 9 requires declaring 'currency exceeding the prescribed amount.' Note: China's own National Immigration Administration, when asked by a foreign traveler how much cash may be carried in, explicitly stated this is a Customs matter, not an immigration matter — confirming Customs (not NIA) is the correct authority for this fact. Undeclared cash above the threshold risks detention and penalties under Customs administrative-penalty rules.

notes: Alcohol of any kind is fully prohibited in Saudi Arabia — it may not be imported, sold, purchased, or consumed anywhere in the Kingdom. Saudi customs officially lists 'alcohol and drugs of all kinds' among prohibited items; possession/importation can lead to seizure, fines, and imprisonment. This is confirmed both by Saudi Arabia's own customs authority (ZATCA) and by the U.S. International Trade Administration's official country commercial guide, which lists alcohol among goods whose importation Saudi law prohibits outright.

legal_source.name: ZATCA (Saudi Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority) – Traveler disclosure & prohibited items guidance

limits.description: Up to 200 cigarettes are duty/tax-free. Quantities exceeding 2,400 cigarettes must go through commercial import procedures and cannot be brought as personal baggage.

notes: Official ZATCA guidance sets a 200-cigarette duty-free personal allowance; larger personal quantities (up to 2,400) are allowed but taxed in full and require SFDA approval, and anything above 2,400 is treated as a commercial import.

legal_source.name: ZATCA (Saudi Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority) – Personal Tobacco Import Quantity Limits for Travelers

CBD isn't named on the pages read, so this row doesn't cover CBD products; ask the authority before travelling with them.

legal_source.name: ZATCA (Saudi Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority) — prohibited items for travelers

notes: ZATCA's page does not name the specific competent authority or describe the approval process/timeline for drones (unlike its more detailed treatment of medicines, which points to the SFDA clearance system cited elsewhere on this site). Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) is the plausible drone/UAV regulator, but that could not be independently confirmed against a primary GACA source in this pass — treat the approval requirement as confirmed, but the exact process as unconfirmed.

Surveillance devices disguised as everyday objects — the source specifically names hidden-camera watches, pens, glasses, and toy airplanes — are also prohibited.

notes: This list is broader and more surveillance/security-focused than a typical 'weapons' list — it groups conventional self-defence items (stun devices, tear gas) with electronic surveillance/countermeasure gear (hidden cameras, radar detectors, eavesdropping devices) and laser pointers above a trivial power threshold.
summary: Banned: stun devices, most laser devices, fireworks, eavesdropping devices, radar detectors and hidden cameras.

legal_source.name: ZATCA (Saudi Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority) — prohibited and restricted items for travelers

limits.description: Article 75 of the Convention Implementing the Schengen Agreement (CISA) lets travelers carry 'the narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances that are necessary for their medical treatment' if, at any check, they can produce a certificate issued or authenticated by a competent authority of their state of residence. Article 75 itself leaves the certificate's exact form and the details on permitted quantity and journey duration to the Schengen Executive Committee. Ireland's Revenue describes the Article 75 certificate as covering a maximum 30-day supply of each prescribed product.
limits.quantity: up to a 30-day supply, evidenced by the Schengen certificate

notes: This is a Schengen-wide legal basis (confirmed directly from Article 75's text), but the certificate itself is issued nationally — by a doctor, pharmacist, or health authority depending on the member state — before you travel; there is no single EU-wide online portal. Article 75 covers 'narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances' as classes rather than naming medicines. On the UN's international lists, amphetamine (Adderall) and methylphenidate (Ritalin) are psychotropic substances, as are alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium) and clonazepam (Klonopin); codeine and oxycodone are narcotic drugs. Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and tramadol are not on those lists, so whether they need a certificate depends on each country's own law. Some Schengen states still restrict or ban specific substances outright under their own national law regardless of the certificate — for example, the UK's own guidance (a non-Schengen state, cited here only as an illustration of the pattern) notes a Schengen certificate cannot be used to bring a Schedule 1 drug into Great Britain. Confirm with the specific member state's narcotics authority before traveling with an unusual medication.
summary: Narcotic or psychotropic medicine needs a certificate from your home country's authority; Ireland says it covers up to 30 days' supply.

limits.description: Kenya Revenue Authority's traveler FAQ lists 'Narcotic drugs' among goods prohibited for import outright (citing the 2nd and 3rd Schedule of the East African Community Customs Management Act), while listing 'Medicaments' generally among restricted goods that may be imported once 'authorization by relevant Government Institutions' is obtained. The FAQ does not say which of these two rules governs a specific controlled prescription medicine (e.g. a stimulant, benzodiazepine, or opioid painkiller), does not name the authorizing institution for medicaments, and states no personal-use quantity or day-supply exception.

notes: This is a genuine, unresolved gap in KRA's public guidance, not a confirmed 'allowed' or 'banned' answer. Kenya's controlling law for scheduled drugs is the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (Control) Act, 1994, and the Pharmacy and Poisons Board is Kenya's medicines regulator, but no traveler-facing page from either body could be reached in this pass (pharmacyboardkenya.org returned an expired-certificate error; NACADA's site had no relevant guidance) to confirm whether a foreign prescription is sufficient or a specific permit is required. Anyone carrying an ADHD stimulant, benzodiazepine, or opioid painkiller should contact a Kenyan diplomatic mission or the Pharmacy and Poisons Board before travel rather than assume the ordinary prescription-medication allowance covers it.
summary: Kenya's customs FAQ lists narcotic drugs as prohibited and medicines as needing authorization, but doesn't say which covers your medicine.

legal_source.name: Kenya Revenue Authority — Passenger Terminal Clearance in Kenya (FAQs)

limits.description: SARS's traveller guide lists 'Narcotics and habit-forming drugs' among prohibited goods that 'may not be imported' at all, while separately stating that 'Travellers may import their personal medicines provided it is for not more than three (3) months' use,' accompanied by a doctor's prescription, under its restricted-goods rule for 'Medicine.' The guide does not specify which rule governs a specific controlled prescription medicine — e.g. an ADHD stimulant, a benzodiazepine, or an opioid painkiller — so it cannot be confirmed from this source alone whether such medication is treated as an allowed personal medicine or a prohibited habit-forming drug.

notes: South Africa separately schedules narcotics/psychotropics under the Medicines and Related Substances Act (Schedules 5 and 6) and the Drugs and Drug Trafficking Act, administered by SAHPRA and SAPS respectively, but no SAHPRA or SAPS page addressing a traveler's personal-use import of scheduled substances could be reached in this pass — SAHPRA's public import-permit pages (importation-of-medical-products-border-control) describe commercial/institutional importation processes, not personal baggage. Given SARS's own guide leaves the 'habit-forming drug' vs 'personal medicine' classification unresolved for controlled prescription drugs, travelers carrying stimulants, benzodiazepines, or opioid painkillers should carry the original prescription plus a doctor's letter and confirm status with SAHPRA or a South African diplomatic mission before travel.
summary: Personal medicine for up to 3 months is allowed with a prescription, but habit-forming drugs are prohibited; the guide doesn't say which applies.

legal_source.name: SARS — SC-PA-01-03 Duty Free Allowances for Travellers (External Guide, Rev. 8, eff. 1 July 2026)

limits.description: "In accordance with Part 101.02.4(1) of the Civil Aviation Regulations, 2011, no remotely [piloted] UAS shall be operated within the Republic of South Africa, unless such UAS has been issued with a certificate of registration by the Director" (South African Civil Aviation Authority). This is a flight-operation registration requirement, not a customs import ban — bringing a drone into the country isn't itself restricted, but legally switching it on to fly is.

notes: SACAA's own UAS guidance page does not address a visitor/tourist exemption, a temporary-registration path, or how a foreign-registered drone is treated — it describes private and commercial operator registration generally, with no carve-out found for short-stay travelers in this pass. Treat flying a personal drone in South Africa as requiring SACAA registration obtained in advance, not something sorted out on arrival; SACAA's own contact for this is rpasInbox@caa.co.za.
summary: You can bring a drone, but you can't fly it until it has a South African Civil Aviation Authority registration certificate.

ANAM doesn't list which medicines count as psychotropic. Amphetamine (Adderall), methylphenidate (Ritalin), alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium) and clonazepam (Klonopin) are psychotropic substances on the UN's international list; we haven't read Mexico's own schedule.

notes: ANAM's traveler-facing text names only 'sustancias psicotrópicas' (psychotropic substances) — it does not mention 'estupefacientes' (narcotic drugs), the separate Mexican legal category that covers opioid painkillers such as codeine, oxycodone, and tramadol. Whether the same simple prescription-only rule extends to opioid painkillers, or whether they instead require the more formal COFEPRIS sanitary import permit used for controlled narcotics (Permiso Sanitario COFEPRIS-03-023, aimed primarily at commercial/institutional importers), is not addressed by ANAM's page, so opioid painkillers are deliberately left out of this entry's name list. limits.description: All of the following are listed by name on the UAE's official controlled/semi-controlled medicines schedule and are allowed for personal use ONLY with supporting documents, up to a maximum 3-month supply: amphetamine (Adderall), lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse), methylphenidate (Ritalin) — Psychotropic Schedule II; alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium), clonazepam (Klonopin) — Psychotropic Schedule IV / 'CD'; codeine, oxycodone — Narcotic Schedule I/II; tramadol — 'CD'. Travelers must carry BOTH a dated, stamped prescription (issued within 3 months) AND an attested medical report (issued within 1 year) naming the medicine, dose, and treatment duration.

notes: The Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) — which took over the Ministry of Health and Prevention's (MOHAP) controlled-medicines functions on 29 Dec 2025 under Federal Decree-Law No. 38 of 2024 — offers an optional electronic pre-approval permit before travel; it is NOT strictly mandatory, and travelers may instead simply declare the medicine with prescription + medical report at the port of entry. This row corrects the common assumption (from older secondary press reporting) that these drugs are outright banned; per EDE's own current list they are not, but the documentation bar (prescription AND medical report, not just prescription alone) is stricter than most countries. This list is dated 15/09/2022 by EDE/MOHAP but remains the current published schedule as of Sept 2026; it explicitly states non-inclusion of a substance doesn't mean it's uncontrolled, so travelers with any other controlled medication should verify against EDE directly. MOHAP's own domain (mohap.gov.ae) was unreachable during this research (connection resets), so EDE.gov.ae — confirmed as the current regulator via the Federal Decree-Law — was used instead.

limits.description: Whether a controlled medicine can be imported depends on which of ANVISA's schedules (Lists A1, A2, A3, B1, B2, C1–C5, set by Portaria SVS/MS n° 344/1998) its active substance is on. Medicines on List C1 may be brought in with only a valid medical prescription shown to the sanitary authority at the port of entry — no advance ANVISA authorization is needed, provided no similar product is registered/sold in Brazil (commercial sale of the imported product is prohibited; personal use only). Medicines on Lists A1, A2, A3, B1, B2, C2 and C5 cannot be imported by a traveler at all without ANVISA's advance, case-by-case 'exceptional use' authorization: the patient/legal guardian must petition before travel through ANVISA's SEI electronic system with a signed prescription (patient name, commercial drug name, dosage, quantity, treatment duration, doctor's signature/CRM), a medical report (diagnosis/CID, case history, justification vs. Brazilian-registered alternatives), and a signed liability statement. Approval is not guaranteed and, once granted, must be presented at the ANVISA airport post to release the medicine.

notes: Substances on List C3 (teratogenic/immunosuppressant, e.g. thalidomide, lenalidomide, pomalidomide) are excluded even from the exceptional-use pathway. Substances on Lists E and F are proscribed outright — import, export, trade and use are illegal for any purpose other than authorized research. This pass verified the mechanism directly from ANVISA's official 'Importação de produtos controlados' page, but did not cross-check the live substance-by-substance annex (Portaria 344/1998, Anexo I, which is amended periodically by separate RDCs) to confirm exactly which list captures each named drug — e.g. whether Adderall/amphetamine, Xanax/alprazolam, Valium/diazepam, Klonopin/clonazepam, codeine, oxycodone or tramadol individually sit on C1 versus one of the prohibited-without-authorization lists. Confirm your specific medicine's list before travel via ANVISA's published substance list or its helpline (0800 642 9782).
summary: Depends on the medicine's ANVISA list: List C1 needs only a valid prescription shown on arrival; Lists A1–A3, B1, B2, C2 and C5 need ANVISA approval first.

limits.description: Medicines containing a substance listed in Appendix A of HSA's 'Document guide for bringing in personal medications' — drawn from the Second and Third Schedules to the Misuse of Drugs Regulations, the First Schedule to the Health Products (Therapeutic Products) Regulations 2016, and other medications of concern — cannot be brought in under the ordinary 3-month traveller allowance. You must submit an online application for HSA approval at least 2 weeks before arrival, in English, attaching medical documentation (pharmacy dispensing label, doctor's prescription, or doctor's letter with patient/prescriber details, medication composition, dose, frequency and total quantity) plus photographs of the product showing its name, active ingredient(s), strength, directions for use, dosage form and dispensed quantity. Approved medications do not need to be declared at customs, but the approval email and supporting documents must be kept available for inspection by ICA officers on request.

notes: Appendix A (edition dated 17 Mar 2026, fetched directly from HSA) explicitly names, among hundreds of substances: Alprazolam, Amphetamine (Amfetamine), Dexamphetamine, Lisdexamphetamine (Vyvanse), Methylphenidate, Dexmethylphenidate, Diazepam, Clonazepam, Codeine, and Oxycodone — so a traveler carrying medicine containing any of these needs HSA approval in advance. Tramadol was checked against the same list and was NOT found on it, so ordinary medicine (not the controlled-substances process) rules appear to apply to it — but confirm against the live Appendix A before travel, since HSA updates it periodically. Cannabis, cannabis extracts, THC, CBD and related cannabinoids are separately and absolutely prohibited under the Fourth Schedule to the Misuse of Drugs Regulations regardless of prescription or approval — Singapore enforces the Misuse of Drugs Act with severe penalties. Modafinil and armodafinil (used for narcolepsy and shift-work sleepiness) are also on Appendix A, so they need HSA approval too.
summary: Medicines on HSA's controlled list need HSA approval, applied for online at least 2 weeks before you arrive.

legal_source.name: Health Sciences Authority (HSA) — Document guide for bringing in personal medications (Appendix A: List of controlled substances)

procedure.title: Get HSA approval before you arrive
procedure.leadTime: At least 2 weeks before you arrive. HSA says later applications may not be processed in time.
documents: Medical documents: a pharmacy dispensing label, a doctor's prescription or a doctor's letter. They must show your and the prescriber's details, the medicine's name and composition, the dose and frequency, and the total quantity prescribed.
Clear photos of the product showing its name, active ingredients, strength, directions for use, dosage form and the quantity dispensed.
steps: Check whether any active ingredient is on Appendix A of HSA's document guide (the list of controlled substances).
Fill in HSA's online application form, in English, at least 2 weeks before you arrive. Incomplete applications are rejected, and you'd have to apply again.
Attach your medical documents and photos as PDF, JPEG or ZIP files.
Keep the approval email. It covers only the arrival date you gave, so if your plans change, apply again.
procedure.atTheBorder: Approved medicines don't need to be declared at customs. Keep the approval email and your documents ready in case immigration (ICA) officers ask to see them.

limits.description: The Singapore Police Force operates a real cross-border cash movement reporting scheme (Form NP 728, lodged with the Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office under the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act) covering cash and bearer negotiable instruments above a threshold.

notes: The specific SGD threshold that triggers mandatory reporting could not be confirmed on a primary source in this pass — the Police e-Services page for lodging the report describes the process (an online form, ~10 minutes to complete) but doesn't state the dollar figure itself, and that page returned no other numeric threshold. If you're carrying a large sum, check the threshold with the Singapore Police Force or file the report anyway.
summary: Cash and bearer negotiable instruments above the threshold must be reported to the Singapore Police Force on Form NP 728.

limits.description: Insulin and GLP-1 medicines (semaglutide, tirzepatide) are not on HSA's Appendix A controlled-substances list, so the drug itself falls under the ordinary personal-medication rule: up to 3 months' supply with a prescription/doctor's letter and original labelled packaging. Separately, delivery hardware — pen injectors, needles and syringes that are not already in use on your body on arrival — may fall under HSA's personal-import-of-medical-devices scheme, which requires its own advance approval (apply at least 10 working days ahead, via a doctor's/dentist's letter confirming and justifying the need), capped at a 3-month supply of devices.

notes: HSA's medical-devices page does not explicitly name insulin pens, injector pens, syringes or needles, and only carves out devices 'already in use when you arrive, such as implanted devices or those already in contact with your skin or eyes' from the approval requirement. It is not clear from the primary source whether a traveler's own in-use insulin pump or GLP-1 pen is exempt on that basis, or whether unopened spare pens/needles/syringes must separately go through the device-import approval — this pass could not resolve that ambiguity from the published text. Confirm directly with HSA (PTM_Enquiry@hsa.gov.sg) before travel, particularly if carrying multiple unopened pens or a supply of needles.
summary: Insulin and GLP-1 medicines: up to 3 months with a prescription. Spare pens, needles and syringes may need separate HSA approval.

legal_source.name: Health Sciences Authority (HSA) — Travelling with medications to Singapore / Travelling with medical devices to Singapore

limits.description: Insulin and GLP-1 injectable drugs (semaglutide/Ozempic/Wegovy, tirzepatide/Mounjaro/Zepbound) are prescription drugs under Japan Customs' general framework: up to a 1-month supply is allowed without a Yakkan Shoumei (import confirmation certificate); a larger supply requires obtaining a Yakkan Shoumei in advance. Injector pens, needles and syringes accompanying the medication are treated as personal-use medical equipment for the same trip.

notes: Japan Customs' 'Private Importation of Drugs, Cosmetics, etc.' FAQ — the same source already used for Japan's general prescription-medication entry — does not separately name insulin, semaglutide/tirzepatide, or syringes/needles/pen injectors; it only gives the general 1-month prescription-drug limit and a separate 'medical equipment' example list (electric massage equipment, low-frequency therapy devices, contact lenses) that does not mention injection devices. No injectable- or device-specific carve-out (e.g. a syringe/needle count cap, or sharps documentation) was found in this pass. For anything beyond routine personal-use quantities, or for questions about needles/syringes specifically, Japan Customs' FAQ directs inquiries to the Regional Bureaus of Health and Welfare (Kanto-Shinetsu: yakkan@mhlw.go.jp; Kinki and west: kiyakuji@mhlw.go.jp).
summary: Up to 1 month's supply of insulin or GLP-1 pens needs no certificate; a larger supply needs a Yakkan Shoumei in advance.

legal_source.name: Japan Customs — Private Importation of Drugs, Cosmetics, etc. (FAQ 1806)

limits.description: Insulin and GLP-1 medicines (semaglutide, tirzepatide) are non-narcotic, non-psychotropic medicines under the Thai FDA's general personal-use rule: they may be carried in the amount necessary for personal use, up to a 30-day supply. Injector pens, needles and syringes used to administer them are medical devices for personal use, which the Thai FDA requires be accompanied by supporting documentation (device information, a purpose letter, and a medical certificate of need).

notes: The Thai FDA's 'Bringing of health products into the Kingdom of Thailand' guidance — the same source already used for Thailand's general medication entry — does not separately name insulin, semaglutide/tirzepatide, or injection devices; it states the general 30-day medicine allowance and a general medical-device documentation requirement, without clarifying how the two interact for an injectable drug delivered via a device (e.g. whether a pen injector needs the medical-device paperwork in addition to a prescription for the medicine inside it). No injectable- or GLP-1-specific carve-out was found in this pass — this is a fast-moving 2026 topic, so confirm current requirements with the Thai FDA or your airline before travel.
summary: Insulin and GLP-1 medicines: up to a 30-day supply. Carry supporting documents for pens, needles and syringes.

limits.description: Insulin, GLP-1 injectable medicines and their delivery devices are covered by Rwanda FDA's personal-effects rule for 'pharmaceutical products and medical devices': the imported quantity must not exceed a 90-day supply (or a single course of treatment) at the maximum manufacturer/healthcare-provider-recommended dose, and import/export should be accompanied by a medical prescription from an authorized practitioner where applicable. The guidelines' definition of 'medical device' ('any instrument, machine, appliance, or material intended by the manufacturer to be used alone or in combination for the purpose of diagnosis, testing, vaccination, cure, surgery or for human or animal health protection') is broad enough to cover pen injectors, needles and syringes used for self-administered injections.

notes: Sourced directly from the same Rwanda FDA Guidelines (FDISM/FDIEC/GDL/003) already used for Rwanda's general prescription-medication and controlled-substances entries — confirmed by parsing the PDF text directly rather than a summarized fetch. The document does not use the words 'insulin,' 'semaglutide,' 'GLP-1' or 'injectable' anywhere — it addresses these products only through the general 'pharmaceutical product' and 'medical device' definitions and the 90-day personal-effects cap — so no insulin/GLP-1-specific guidance (e.g. a distinct sharps or needle-count rule) exists on this primary source. Products 'that require direct oversight or administration by a trained operator' additionally require the importer to provide the contact details of the Rwandan health facility/provider who will administer them — self-injected insulin/GLP-1 pens would not normally fall in that category, but this was not explicitly confirmed for these specific products. The cited Rwanda FDA guideline was due for review on 14 March 2026, and the file was offline when we re-checked on 17 October 2026, so confirm with Rwanda FDA before you travel.
summary: Insulin and GLP-1 pens: up to a 90-day supply or one course of treatment, with a prescription where applicable.

limits.description: Individuals may cross the U.S. border with a Schedule II-V controlled substance for personal medical use if (1) it is in the original container it was dispensed in, and (2) the traveler declares it to a CBP officer, stating either the trade/chemical name and schedule, or the prescribing practitioner/pharmacy and prescription number. U.S. residents bringing such medication back into the U.S. after obtaining it abroad are capped at 50 dosage units combined across all such medication; that cap does not apply to medication lawfully obtained in the U.S. before departure, and the source does not state it applying to non-resident visitors entering with their own foreign prescription.
limits.quantity: 50 dosage units (U.S. residents only, for meds obtained abroad)

notes: This is a DEA regulation (21 CFR 1301.26), separate from CBP's 90-day-supply guidance on the site's general 'prescription medication' entry -- the two operate together. Under the DEA's schedules, Schedule II (21 CFR 1308.12) lists amphetamine (Adderall), methylphenidate (Ritalin), lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse), oxycodone and codeine, and Schedule IV (21 CFR 1308.14) lists alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium), clonazepam (Klonopin), tramadol and modafinil, so all fall within the II-V range this exemption covers. The regulation text itself does not name these drugs by brand, only by schedule.
summary: Controlled medicine is allowed for personal use if it's in its original container and you declare it to CBP.

limits.description: As FDA-approved prescription drugs, GLP-1 medications (semaglutide/tirzepatide) and insulin follow the FDA's personal importation framework: the FDA "will allow foreign nationals to bring or ship a 90-day supply of drug products". For medication sent by mail or courier, the FDA suggests including documentation such as a copy of your visa/passport, a letter from your doctor, or a copy of the prescription in English.

notes: Compounded or non-FDA-approved semaglutide/tirzepatide products are treated differently: FDA's personal importation policy only extends discretionary allowance to unapproved drugs when there's a serious condition, no domestic availability, no unreasonable risk, and written affirmation of personal use. Genuine brand-name Ozempic/Wegovy/Mounjaro/Zepbound are FDA-approved, so this stricter unapproved-drug pathway shouldn't apply to them, but a compounded version should expect more scrutiny. Airport security screening of pens and needles is a separate matter, handled by the TSA, and is not covered here.
summary: Visitors can bring or ship up to a 90-day supply of insulin or FDA-approved GLP-1 medicine.

limits.description: Up to 3 months' supply of medicine containing a controlled drug can be carried in hand luggage without a Home Office licence. All of the stimulants, benzodiazepines and opioids named in this entry are Schedule 2-4 drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations (amphetamine, methylphenidate and lisdexamfetamine: Schedule 2; oxycodone: Schedule 2; codeine: Schedule 2 or 5 depending on the preparation; tramadol: Schedule 3; diazepam, alprazolam and clonazepam: Schedule 4 Part 1), so the 3-month exemption applies to them -- only Schedule 1 drugs are barred without a special licence. Non-UK residents must carry a letter stating their name, travel dates, and a list of the medicine with dose/strength, signed by the prescriber; the medicine must travel in hand luggage, not hold luggage.

notes: The Home Office's personal import policy covers medicine lawfully prescribed to you in the country where you normally live, carried on your person. It doesn't apply to UK residents who were prescribed controlled drugs while abroad: they must email the Drug and Firearms Licensing Unit (DFLU, dflu.ie@homeoffice.gov.uk) before returning. Staying longer than 3 months: bring up to 3 months' supply and see a UK clinician for more; medicine containing controlled drugs can't be posted to you, and excess quantities are seized. Schedule 1 drugs can't be imported without a licence, which is limited to research or special purposes; a Schengen certificate doesn't replace it.

limits.description: Under CBSA's Section 56 Class Exemption, travelers may personally carry (in person only -- not by mail or courier) a prescribed narcotic or Food and Drug Regulations Part G controlled drug up to the lesser of a single course of treatment or a 30-day supply, and a prescribed benzodiazepine/targeted substance up to the lesser of a single course of treatment or a 90-day supply. If you don't live in Canada, the benzodiazepine limit is the lesser of the container's contents, a 90-day supply, or your usual daily dose multiplied by the number of days you plan to stay. Opioids (codeine, oxycodone, tramadol) and stimulants (amphetamine, methylphenidate/Ritalin, lisdexamfetamine/Vyvanse) fall under the narcotic/Part-G 30-day limit; benzodiazepines (diazepam/Valium, alprazolam/Xanax, clonazepam/Klonopin) get the 90-day limit. Medication must be in pharmacy- or hospital-dispensed packaging with proper labelling, and must be declared to a CBSA officer at the border.

notes: No advance import permit is required for these amounts under the Class Exemption -- but it does not cover Annex I-listed substances unless separately approved by Health Canada or the source country's regulator, and it explicitly does not apply to shipping controlled substances by mail or courier, only carrying them in person. Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) isn't named in the Act; we treat it as covered by Schedule I's "amphetamines, their salts, derivatives…" entry, which is our reading.
summary: Carry it in person: up to 30 days of stimulants or opioids, 90 days of benzodiazepines, in labelled packaging. Declare it.

limits.description: GLP-1 drugs and insulin are ordinary (non-controlled) prescription drugs in Canada, so the general personal-use rule applies: a single course of treatment or a 90-day supply, whichever is less, hand-carried in original/clearly labelled pharmacy packaging. This applies to visitors, and to residents of Canada returning with pens or insulin prescribed and filled in Canada; residents generally may not bring in prescription drugs prescribed or bought abroad. Health Canada's guidance separately states that medical devices imported for personal use -- which covers self-administered injection pens, syringes and needles -- are not restricted under the Food and Drugs Act or Medical Devices Regulations, provided the device doesn't require a trained operator, i.e. it's meant for the patient's own self-administration.

notes: This guidance document does not mention insulin, GLP-1 drugs, needles or syringes by name -- the 90-day rule is the same generic prescription-drug provision already used for the site's general prescription-medication-ca entry, and the needle/syringe treatment is inferred from the document's general 'medical devices for personal use' section, not a dedicated sharps policy. No refrigeration/cold-chain guidance was found on this source.
summary: Insulin and GLP-1 pens: a 90-day supply or one course of treatment, whichever is less, in labelled pharmacy packaging.

limits.description: Australia's traveller's exemption lets you bring up to 3 months' supply of your prescription medicine, and the Office of Drug Control confirms this covers Schedule 8-type medicines too: 'Prescription medicines such as morphine, oxycodone, methadone, methylphenidate, Adderall, and benzodiazepines are all covered by the traveller exemption.' Codeine-containing medication is also covered but 'requires a prescription from your medical doctor.' You need a valid prescription or a doctor's letter stating the medicine name and dosage, and the medicine should stay in its original packaging with the dispensing label intact; declare everything to the Australian Border Force on arrival.

notes: If you need more than 3 months' worth, ODC's guidance points to either getting a new prescription from an Australian-registered prescriber, or importing a further 3-month supply if the medicine isn't otherwise restricted -- it does not describe an advance import-permit process for a longer personal supply of these particular drugs, unlike Thailand's or Japan's schemes. Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is not named individually on this source (only 'methylphenidate' and 'Adderall' are used as the stimulant examples) and so is omitted from this entry's names, even though it is a similar stimulant class. Methadone is also named as covered by the source but isn't included here since it wasn't part of the requested drug list.
summary: Up to 3 months' supply, including Adderall, Ritalin, oxycodone and benzodiazepines, with a prescription or doctor's letter. Declare it.

Carry them in your accompanied baggage, with a letter from your doctor or a copy of your prescription in English. Keep them in the original packaging, bring no more than 3 months' supply, and declare them.

notes: You need a permit from the Office of Drug Control if you don't have a prescription, if you're bringing more than 3 months' supply, or if you're an athlete. The athlete rule also covers support staff, such as a coach, doctor or manager, coming to Australia for an athlete's work, and applies even with a prescription. Without a permit, the Border Force can seize the goods, and you can face an on-the-spot fine or prosecution.
summary: Allowed without a permit only if prescribed to you: up to 3 months, with a prescription or doctor's letter in English. Declare it.

limits.description: Without a prescription: don't bring them. Australia's Poisons Standard lists BPC-157, TB-500 (thymosin beta-4), ipamorelin, CJC-1295, GHRP-6, GHRP-2, hexarelin, AOD-9604, ibutamoren and Melanotan II as prescription-only medicines (Schedule 4). All but Melanotan II are also on its list of medicines that are illegal to possess without authority. A traveller's personal supply of a Schedule 4 medicine is only exempt if a doctor has given written authority, such as a prescription. A doctor overseas counts. With one: carry the prescription or a doctor's letter in English, bring no more than 3 months' supply in packaging that identifies the medicine, and declare it.

notes: Athletes, and sporting staff travelling with them, need written permission from the Office of Drug Control to bring hormones and peptides, even with a prescription. limits.description: "Some plants and animals are protected under international law. This includes items made from endangered species. NZ Customs names corals, clams, crocodile products, and certain traditional medicines as commonly seized items; the Department of Conservation issues permits (where obtainable at all) for ivory products, animal skins, leather goods, furs, shells, marine life items, protected timber, and live species.

notes: This is a CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species) enforcement matter, not a simple customs allowance — many categories named here (ivory in particular) have no realistic personal-import permit path even when a permit process technically exists. limits.description: Under Dangerous Drugs Board Regulation No. 1, Series of 2014, Section 35, a traveler entering, leaving, or passing through the Philippines who is under treatment for a medical condition may possess a dangerous drug or a drug preparation containing a controlled chemical, in a quantity reasonable for that treatment, when prescribed by a valid PDEA S2-licensed physician. For a supply of up to 30 days, the traveler must carry: (a) a letter from the attending physician describing the medical condition, (b) the physician's prescription listing the trade and generic names of the drug, and the medicine in its original, properly labeled container — no advance PDEA permit is required for this 30-day case.

For a supply exceeding 30 days, the traveler additionally needs Certificates of Authorization from PDEA and from the National Competent Authority of their home country (incoming) or destination country (outgoing); the PDEA request must be submitted in writing at least 30 working days before travel, and PDEA replies within 15 working days.

notes: The regulation governs 'dangerous drugs' and 'drug preparations containing a controlled chemical' generally (as scheduled under RA 9165, the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002) rather than naming specific brands like Adderall or Xanax; it does not itself state which named medicines fall in which schedule. Amphetamine, methylphenidate, diazepam, alprazolam, clonazepam, codeine and oxycodone are on the UN's international control lists; confirm their specific medicine's PH classification with PDEA before travel. Outgoing travelers must also check the destination country's own requirements.

limits.description: The Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP) states plainly: "There is no special permit required for flying drones for recreational purposes." Operating rules apply instead of a permit: keep the drone within visual line of sight, stay at or below 120m/400ft altitude, stay at least 10km from any airport's movement area, don't fly at night, over crowds, over national-security-sensitive government facilities, or in any area with an active fire/police/emergency response. Travelers should also check with the Local Government Unit (LGU) of the area for local drone ordinances, which CAAP notes can add restrictions on top of the national rules.

notes: A genuinely different, more permissive answer than most destinations checked for this category — Philippines has no registration or advance-permit requirement for personal/recreational drones, only in-flight operating rules. Commercial drone operations are separately gated behind a CAAP Certificate of Authorization (COA), which doesn't apply to a tourist's personal use.
summary: No permit is needed to fly a drone for fun, but CAAP rules apply: line of sight, 120 m maximum, 10 km from airports, no night flights.
