limits.description: You must declare money worth 50,000 NIS or more (combined) when entering or leaving Israel. The threshold is 12,000 NIS for entering or leaving Gaza and for leaving Israel by land (Rafah, Nitzana, Jordan River, Yitzhak Rabin crossings); at the Allenby crossing it is the equivalent of 2,000 Jordanian dinars.

notes: Israel Tax Authority, 'Money laundering' (Required Reporting of Transfer of Money into and out of Israel; page updated 28.06.2021), under the Prohibition of Money Laundering Law, 2000 and its 2001 reporting regulations. 'Money' means cash, cashier's cheques, traveller's cheques, bearer securities, negotiable instruments and payment cards. You declare on Customs form 84a. Not declaring is an offence: up to 6 months in prison or a fine of up to ten times the undeclared amount, whichever is higher. Police and customs can seize the amount above the threshold. The 50,000 NIS general threshold dates from the 7 December 2017 amendment to section 4 of the law. Carrying money is allowed; only the declaration is required.

legal_source.name: Money laundering — Required Reporting of Transfer of Money into and out of Israel, Israel Tax Authority (gov.il)

limits.description: You may bring medicines for your own normal personal needs, up to a 90-day supply at the recommended dosage. This does not cover narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, which have separate rules (see controlled-medication-il).

notes: Israel Ministry of Health, Pharmaceutics Division: 'Travelers entering Israel can bring medicines in amounts that are suitable to their own personal needs. This personal supply is limited to a maximum 90-day quantity based on the recommended dosage for each medication. However, this does not apply to narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances.' Israeli law applies even if the product is not a medicine where you bought it: supplements or vitamins sold over the counter abroad 'may be classified as medicines requiring authorization in Israel', especially if they are marketed with medical claims. The page does not say whether a prescription must be carried for non-controlled medicines.

legal_source.name: International Travel with Controlled Substances — Guidelines for Travelers, Pharmaceutics Division, Israel Ministry of Health (gov.il; English page updated 28.05.2024, Hebrew version updated 30.08.2026)

limits.description: Medicines with substances listed in the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance may be brought into Israel in amounts for up to 31 days. You must carry a photocopy of a valid prescription, the medicine in its original package, and a 'permit to carry a controlled substance' issued by the health authority of your country of residence.

notes: Israel Ministry of Health: 'Substances specified in the Controlled Substances Ordinance may be brought into Israel in amounts sufficient for 31 days. To comply with the Ordinance, travelers must carry the following: 1. A photocopy of a valid prescription, 2. Medicine in its original package, 3. "A permit to carry a controlled substance" issued by the competent health authority in the country of residence.' The Hebrew version (updated 30.08.2026) says the same: 31 days, with the same three documents. Israel's INCB country form (dated 04.12.2023) matches: 31 days each for narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, a valid prescription, a doctor's certificate endorsed by the home health authority, the original container, and a traveller's certificate for narcotic/psychotropic medicines endorsed by the home health authorities. Contact: Ministry of Health Pharmaceutical Division, rok.import@moh.gov.il / PERMITS@MOH.GOV.IL, tel. 08-6241010. The drugs named here (opioids, methylphenidate, benzodiazepines) come from the page's UNODC table of controlled substances. That table is advice for Israelis travelling abroad, not an Israeli import limit; the Israeli limit is the 31-day rule. The page does not say how amphetamine-based ADHD medicines such as Adderall are treated on entry, so check with the Ministry of Health. Cannabis is not covered here (see unverified).

legal_source.name: International Travel with Controlled Substances — Guidelines for Travelers, Pharmaceutics Division, Israel Ministry of Health (gov.il; English page updated 28.05.2024, Hebrew version updated 30.08.2026)

limits.description: Importing a drone needs approval from the competent authorities (Ministry of Communications, and Ministry of Transportation / Israel Airports Authority). Tourists must also leave a guarantee equal to the applicable taxes, refunded when they take the drone out of Israel.

notes: Israel Tax Authority tourist customs guide, 'Items which Import is Conditional on the Approval of the Competent Authority': Drone — Ministry of Communications, Ministry of Transportation - Israel Airports Authority (03-5198282, requests@moc.gov.il; 03-9774521, gendela@mot.gov.il). An import approval can be obtained before or after the item arrives, but the item is only released after it is presented. An import licence must be obtained before arrival, and failing to do so is an offence that may bring a fine. 'Taxes and Guarantees' chapter: 'If you have brought with you one of the following items: a new personal computer, a UAV (drone), electric bicycle or similar items, you will be required to deposit a guarantee in the amount of taxes applicable to them - in cash or by credit card.' The guarantee is returned if you take the item out on time, and kept if you don't. Declare in the red channel. Flying rules inside Israel are not covered here.
summary: Drones need approval from Israel's communications and transport authorities, and tourists leave a refundable tax guarantee.

legal_source.name: Customs Guide for Tourists and Foreign Residents — Israel Tax Authority (gov.il), chapter 'Items which Import is Conditional on the Approval of the Competent Authority' (updated 30.07.2026)

limits.description: Weapons and weapon parts need approval from the Ministry of Public Security. Some items are banned outright, including knives other than pocket knives or knives for a legitimate trade or household purpose, gun-shaped tear gas canisters, starting pistols or gas-operated firearms and similar tools, explosives, and radar/laser jammer detectors.

notes: Israel Tax Authority tourist customs guide: 'Weapon and parts — Ministry of Public Security, 077-2324444' is on the list of items whose import needs a competent authority's approval. The prohibited-items chapter lists, among others: 'A knife, other than a pocket knife and other than a knife intended for the usage in a profession, craft, business, household or any other legitimate purpose; A Radar Laser Jammer Detector; A wrap-like firearm (gun wrap pistol skin) or starting pistol-like or a gas-operated firearm or any similar tools; A tear gas canister, shaped like a firearm; ... Explosives and flammable substances'. The guide calls these 'examples', so the list is not complete. Pepper spray in non-firearm form and tasers are not specifically addressed.

legal_source.name: Customs Guide for Tourists and Foreign Residents — Israel Tax Authority (gov.il), chapter 'Items that are prohibited for importation' (updated 30.07.2026)

limits.description: Plants and seeds need a plant protection certificate/approval from the Ministry of Agriculture before customs will release them. Used sacks or wrapping that held plant material are banned.

notes: Israel Tax Authority tourist customs guide, approvals list: 'Plants, seeds — Ministry of Agriculture – plant protection certificate, 03-9681587, Beit Dagan'. The prohibited-items list includes 'Used sacks or any other wrapping material that were used for packaging vegetative material' and 'Used apiculture (beekeeping) equipment'. The guide does not specifically say how fresh fruit and vegetables are treated, and the Ministry of Agriculture's own traveller page could not be found, so fruit and vegetables are left out of this row (see unverified). Separately, the green channel allows food within the $200 personal allowance, up to 3 kg in total and no more than 1 kg of each type, but only for food that needs no approval.

legal_source.name: Customs Guide for Tourists and Foreign Residents — Israel Tax Authority (gov.il), chapter 'Items which Import is Conditional on the Approval of the Competent Authority' (updated 30.07.2026)

limits.description: Duty-free: other goods for personal use or as gifts worth up to US$200 per entrant aged 2 or over, which can include food up to 3 kg in total (max 1 kg per type); perfume up to 250 ml. Used, portable personal items (camera, laptop, jewellery, sports or camping gear, etc.) may pass the green channel but must leave with you. New computers, drones and e-bikes need a tax guarantee.

notes: Israel Tax Authority: the exemption 'is strictly personal to each of the entrants' and allowances can't be combined. 'If the value of an imported item exceeds $200, it is not possible to get an exemption for $200 and pay taxes on the difference. Entrants will be charged taxes on the full value of the item.' Use the red channel if in doubt, or for portable work tools, diving equipment, e-bikes or a new computer. Customs may ask for a guarantee for some items. There is no exemption for items sent by parcel post.
summary: Up to US$200 of goods duty-free per traveller aged 2+, including food up to 3 kg. New drones and laptops need a tax guarantee.

legal_source.name: Customs Guide for Tourists and Foreign Residents — Israel Tax Authority (gov.il), chapter 'The green channel Passage with Tax-Exempt Items' (updated 30.07.2026)

limits.description: Banned: counterfeit or obscene goods; counterfeit coins or documents; unlicensed lottery/gambling tickets and adverts; forbidden games; dangerous live animals such as vipers; tools used to make or consume a dangerous drug; goods that may incite violence, terrorism or racism or show support for a terrorist organisation.

notes: Israel Tax Authority tourist customs guide, 'Items that are prohibited for importation' (these are 'examples', so the list is not complete): 'Goods that are hacked or obscene; Counterfeits and imitations of coins and of documents; Tickets and advertisements for lotteries or gambling, for which performance no permit has been issued in advance; ... Forbidden games; Explosives and flammable substances, living creatures such as vipers and similar dangerous goods; Used apiculture (beekeeping) equipment; Goods, which are tools of the kind used to make or consume a dangerous drug; Goods, which have the potential to incite violence, terrorism or racism; Goods, which have a manifestation of identification with or sympathy for a terrorist organization.'

legal_source.name: Customs Guide for Tourists and Foreign Residents — Israel Tax Authority (gov.il), chapter 'Items that are prohibited for importation' (updated 30.07.2026)

notes: This covers peptides that are not FDA-approved drugs, such as BPC-157, TB-500, melanotan II, CJC-1295, ipamorelin and retatrutide. The FDA says that if a drug is not approved in the US, importing it is illegal, even for personal use and even if it is approved in another country. A "research use only" or "not for human consumption" label does not change this: in a March 2026 warning letter the FDA said such labels do not stop a product being treated as a drug for human use. The FDA may let a personal supply through in limited cases (generally no more than 3 months, for your own use, and for a serious condition with no treatment available in the US, or a product with no known significant health risk). That is a choice the FDA makes, not a right, and the FDA has flagged safety concerns for most of the peptides named here. FDA-approved peptide medicines, such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro or insulin, are a different case: see the injectable medication entry.

notes: Health Canada says peptides are generally regulated as prescription drugs in Canada, and unauthorized drug products are illegal. Its April 2026 advisory names BPC-157, CJC-1295, DSIP, epitalon, GHK-Cu, ipamorelin, KPV, melanotan I and II, MOTS-c, SS-31, TB-500 and retatrutide among products it has seized, and says a "for research use only" label does not make a product legal. An authorized drug has an eight-digit Drug Identification Number (DIN) on the label. Health Canada works with the Canada Border Services Agency to stop unauthorized shipments. An authorized peptide medicine prescribed to you is a different case: visitors may bring a personal quantity of a prescription drug for their own use (no more than a 90-day supply or one course of treatment, whichever is less), and residents of Canada may bring back a drug prescribed and filled in Canada, but generally not one prescribed or bought abroad. See the prescription medication entry.

limits.description: Without a prescription: not allowed. Medsafe says many peptide products are prescription medicines under the Medicines Act 1981, and it is unlawful to import, supply or possess them unless this is authorised. With a prescription: the normal rule for prescription medicines applies. Bring no more than 3 months' supply, carry a copy of your prescription or a letter from your doctor, keep it in the original containers, and declare it on your arrival card.

notes: Medsafe's May 2026 advisory names BPC-157, CJC-1295, GHRP-6, ipamorelin, kisspeptin, KLOW, melanotan II, retatrutide, selank, semax, TB-500 and thymosin, and says the list is not complete. It says wording such as "for research purposes only" has no legal effect. Having peptides posted or couriered to you is stricter than carrying them: you need an original prescription or letter from a New Zealand prescriber, and the 3-month limit still applies.

limits.description: Melatonin bought overseas, such as a US supplement, is an unapproved medicine in New Zealand. Medsafe says you still need a prescription to import unapproved melatonin for personal use. With a prescription, New Zealand's normal rule for prescription medicine applies: bring no more than 3 months' supply, carry a copy of the prescription or a letter from your doctor, keep it in the original containers, and declare it on your arrival card.

notes: Since June 2025 New Zealand pharmacies can supply some approved melatonin medicines without a prescription: up to 10 days' supply for jet lag and up to 30 days for insomnia. That covers only products approved in New Zealand, not supplements you bring from abroad.
summary: Needs a prescription to bring in. With one, up to 3 months' supply, declared on arrival.

limits.description: Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) is a prescription medicine in New Zealand, and it isn't allowed in herbal remedies or dietary supplements. Medsafe says kratom for personal use that's found at the border is referred to Medsafe, and released only on the authority of a medical practitioner, who takes responsibility for it.

notes: Kratom isn't approved for any kind of medical use in New Zealand. Without a doctor's authority, Medsafe won't release it.

legal_source.name: Medsafe Prescriber Update — Kratom: not such a nice cup of tea (2 December 2021)

limits.description: All medicines containing pseudoephedrine are controlled drugs in New Zealand, including cold and flu medicines you can buy without a prescription elsewhere. Declare them on your New Zealand Traveller Declaration, keep them in their original packaging and in your hand luggage, and bring no more than one month's supply. Customs' controlled-drug rules also ask for a copy of your prescription or a letter from your doctor confirming you're being treated with it, with its name and strength.

notes: You can't bring pseudoephedrine medicines into New Zealand for friends or family. Check the label of any cold or allergy medicine you pack: if it lists pseudoephedrine, these rules apply.

legal_source.name: New Zealand Customs Service — Prohibited and restricted items (travellers)

limits.description: Growth hormone (somatropin, somatotropin, somatrem) and HCG are controlled drugs in Schedule 4 Part 2 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001. The law allows you to bring them in person for your own use. Carry them in your hand luggage, bring no more than 3 months' supply, and if you don't live in the UK, carry a letter signed by your prescriber with your name, travel dates, and the medicine's name, amount, dose and strength. Medicine you can't prove was prescribed to you may be seized.

notes: The exemption only covers bringing it yourself, for yourself. Having growth hormone or HCG posted or couriered to you from abroad is not covered, and gov.uk says medicine sent to you by post will be taken away. Peptides that are not on this list, such as BPC-157 or TB-500, are not covered by this entry.
summary: Allowed in person, in hand luggage, up to 3 months' supply. Non-residents need a letter from the prescriber.

legal_source.name: Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, regulation 4(2) and Schedule 4 Part 2 (legislation.gov.uk)

limits.description: Melatonin is a prescription-only medicine in the UK. It's licensed for short-term insomnia and jet lag in adults, and for some sleep disorders in children aged 6 to 17. It isn't legally sold as a food supplement there: products containing it are regulated as medicines and need a marketing authorisation.

notes: UK government guidance on travelling with medicine covers controlled drugs. We found no official UK rule on how much of a prescription-only medicine that isn't a controlled drug, such as melatonin, you can bring for personal use, or what proof you need. So we can't confirm a limit. Don't plan on buying melatonin in UK shops.
summary: Prescription-only in the UK; it isn't sold as a food supplement there.

limits.description: Only if a doctor prescribed it to you. HSA lets travellers bring up to 3 months' supply of a medicine without prior approval when it was lawfully prescribed to you in your country of residence, you carry a copy of the prescription or a doctor's letter, and it stays in its original container labelled by the dispensing pharmacy. More than 3 months' supply is not allowed. Peptide vials bought online without a prescription don't meet these conditions.

notes: HSA says retatrutide and cagrilintide are unapproved injectable peptides still in clinical development, and that no regulator, including HSA, has approved them as medicines. It also says labels such as "research use only" or "not for human consumption" should be treated as a warning sign. Approved GLP-1 medicines such as semaglutide and tirzepatide are a different case: see the injectable medication entry, which also covers bringing pens, needles and syringes.
summary: Only if prescribed to you: up to 3 months' supply, with a copy of the prescription or a doctor's letter, in the original pharmacy-labelled container.

limits.description: Don't bring it. Kratom's active compounds, mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine, are Class A controlled drugs under Singapore's Misuse of Drugs Act. Importing kratom carries at least 5 years in prison and 5 strokes of the cane, and up to 30 years or life imprisonment and 15 strokes.

notes: Possessing kratom can mean up to 10 years in prison, a fine of up to S$20,000, or both. Consuming it is a separate offence: at least 1 year and up to 10 years in prison, and a fine of up to S$20,000.
summary: Banned: kratom's active compounds are Class A drugs in Singapore. Importing it carries at least 5 years in prison and 5 strokes of the cane.

legal_source.name: Central Narcotics Bureau — Kratom

limits.description: Don't bring it. Singapore's Health Sciences Authority doesn't allow personal imports of medications in chewing gum form under any circumstances. That includes nicotine gum used to quit smoking.

notes: This entry covers medicated gum under HSA's personal-medication rules. Ordinary chewing gum is banned separately (see chewing gum). Other forms of nicotine replacement, such as patches, have their own rules that we haven't verified yet.
summary: Banned: Singapore doesn't allow personal imports of medicines in chewing-gum form, including nicotine gum.

legal_source.name: Health Sciences Authority — Travelling with medications to Singapore (last updated 15 June 2026)

limits.description: Don't bring it. Singapore prohibits importing any chewing gum. The only exceptions are gum registered under the Health Products Act as a therapeutic product (other than a general-sale medicine) or as an oral dental gum meeting set composition rules. There's no allowance for travellers.

notes: Breaking the rules can mean a fine of up to S$100,000 or up to 2 years in prison on a first conviction, and up to S$200,000 or 3 years for a repeat offence. The only other permits are for commercial transit to Malaysia, transhipment and registered manufacturers' research. Medicated gum, such as nicotine gum, also can't be brought in under HSA's personal-medication rules.
summary: Banned: you can't bring chewing gum into Singapore, apart from registered therapeutic or dental gums. Fines up to S$100,000.

legal_source.name: Regulation of Imports and Exports (Chewing Gum) Regulations, regs 3, 3A, 4 and 7 (Singapore Statutes Online, current version)

limits.description: Bringing a medical device into Singapore for personal use needs HSA approval first, unless it's already in use when you arrive (for example an implanted device, or one already in contact with your skin or eyes). Each approval covers at most 3 months' supply; larger imports are rejected. For a device your doctor or dentist prescribed, you need their letter confirming and justifying the need.

notes: Not allowed through personal import at all: HIV test kits; radiation-emitting devices (for example X-ray, laser or ultrasound) that are potentially hazardous or meant for use by trained medical personnel; and devices to be administered by a qualified practitioner. You don't need to declare approved devices on arrival, but keep the supporting documents and the approval email with you for customs checks during your stay, and take the devices with you when you leave. You may not sell or give them to anyone except the family members they were meant for. HSA's page doesn't list device types (such as CPAP machines or glucose monitors) by name.
summary: Needs HSA approval at least 10 working days ahead, unless the device is already in use on you. Up to 3 months' supply.

procedure.title: Get HSA approval for a medical device
procedure.leadTime: At least 10 working days before you arrive.
documents: If the device was prescribed to you: a letter from your doctor or dentist confirming and justifying your need for it.
steps: Check the device isn't one HSA excludes from personal import: HIV test kits, hazardous radiation-emitting devices, and devices to be administered by a qualified practitioner.
Submit HSA's online personal-import form for medical devices at least 10 working days before you arrive. Applications are reviewed case by case.
Get the approval before you start travelling. Each approval covers up to 3 months' supply.
Keep the approval email and your documents with you during your stay, and take the device with you when you leave.
procedure.atTheBorder: You don't need to declare approved devices, but customs officers may ask to see the approval email and your documents.

transit.description: You don't need HSA approval for a medical device if you stay within the transit zones while transiting Singapore.

notes: The Thai FDA's page doesn't name device types or set a numeric limit. Products that are legally prohibited from import into Thailand can't be brought in this way.

notes: These are the personal-import limits under Japan's Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Act, which lets you import for personal use without a business licence only within these limits. Japan Customs refers questions about anything beyond them to a special pharmaceutical inspector at a Regional Bureau of Health and Welfare (for Tokyo, Yokohama and Hakodate: yakkan@mhlw.go.jp). The page doesn't name other device types, such as CPAP machines or glucose monitors.

limits.description: Medical devices for personal use are exempt from device registration, the establishment licence and the customs import permit, under the Medical Device (Exemption) Order 2024. They must be for you or your immediate family only, not for sale or distribution, and keep all their original labels. Quantity depends on the type: low- or medium-risk devices (for example glucose monitoring devices, hearing aids, in-vitro diagnostic products): 1 piece of each type; consumables (for example contact lenses, test strips): up to 3 months' supply.
limits.quantity: 1 piece of each low/medium-risk device; 3 months' supply of consumables

notes: The Medical Device Authority (MDA) may ask for a formal prescription or a letter of recommendation from a registered healthcare professional; some device types don't need one. MDA also lists as a requirement that no same or similar device is registered in Malaysia (search the MDA register at mdar.mda.gov.my). Questions go to the MDA's Policy and Strategic Planning Division (+603 8230 0253).
summary: Personal-use devices need no permit: 1 of each device (e.g. a glucose monitor or hearing aid), 3 months of consumables.

legal_source.name: Medical Device Authority (Malaysia) — Personal Use Medical Device (uploaded 10 July 2026)

limits.description: Travellers can bring these medical devices for personal use without special approval from the TFDA, each category at most once every 6 months: adhesive bandages, up to 60 pieces; liquid bandage, up to 4 tubes (jars, bottles, units); cotton swabs, up to 200; condoms, up to 60; tampons, up to 120; daily disposable contact lenses, 60 per diopter, one brand and two diopters per person; corrective lenses, 1 pair; medical masks, up to 250.
limits.quantity: per-item caps; each category once every 6 months

notes: These limits come from Article 6, Paragraph 4 of the Regulations Governing Special Approval for Manufacture or Import of Specific Medical Devices. The TFDA's page lists only these items; it doesn't say how other devices (such as CPAP machines or glucose monitors) are treated. Devices brought in this way may not be sold, transferred or given to anyone else; selling them can mean a fine of NT$30,000 to NT$1,000,000 under the Medical Devices Act.
summary: Listed items only, with caps (e.g. 60 daily contact lenses per diopter, 250 medical masks), once every 6 months per category.

legal_source.name: Taiwan Food and Drug Administration — Be careful when bringing medical devices into Taiwan for personal use (updated 6 July 2026)

limits.description: Prescription medicines that don't contain controlled drugs: bring a copy of your prescription or a letter from your doctor confirming you're being treated with the medicine, keep it in its original packaging, and bring no more than three months' supply. Oral contraceptives: up to six months' supply.
limits.quantity: 3 months' supply (6 months for oral contraceptives)

notes: NZ Customs says prescription medicines and controlled drugs must be declared on the New Zealand Traveller Declaration, and lists two cases where you must declare prescription medicine: you're carrying more than three months' supply, or the medicine isn't prescribed to you or a family member. Medicines containing controlled drugs, including all medicines containing pseudoephedrine, have stricter rules (see the controlled-medication and pseudoephedrine entries). Customs points to Medsafe for non-prescription medicines.
summary: Up to 3 months' supply (6 for oral contraceptives), in original packaging, with a prescription copy or doctor's letter.

legal_source.name: New Zealand Customs Service -- Prohibited and restricted items: medicines

limits.description: Travellers may bring their personal medication into Spain (Art. 74, Royal Legislative Decree 1/2015), and AEMPS recommends carrying a prescription or doctor's report. Narcotic or psychotropic medicine under international control also needs a certificate or permit from the Spanish health authorities authorising its entry into Spain. AEMPS takes at least 10 days to process it, and it's valid for at most 3 months. The maximum quantity for travel to Spain is three months of treatment (15 days for cannabis or its derivatives).
limits.quantity: up to 3 months of treatment (15 days for cannabis)

notes: This is Spain's national rule, set out by AEMPS. The page doesn't say how it applies to someone arriving from another Schengen country with an Article 75 certificate issued by their own country (see the EU entry). Patients on opioid substitution treatment (methadone or buprenorphine) apply through a drug-treatment centre (CAD) or another authorised body, not by themselves. Brand names are listed for search only: they map to substances on the UN's international control lists.
summary: Narcotic or psychotropic medicine needs an AEMPS permit; apply at least 10 days ahead. Up to 3 months of treatment.

procedure.title: Get an AEMPS permit to bring narcotic or psychotropic medicine into Spain
procedure.authority: Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices (AEMPS)
procedure.leadTime: At least 10 days before you travel
procedure.processingTime: At least 10 days, if everything is complete
documents: The completed, signed application form.
An up-to-date medical certificate, signed and stamped, with the doctor's name, registration number, address and phone, your condition, the treatment and the daily dose.
Your current original prescription, signed by the prescriber.
A copy of your passport.
A copy of your travel tickets (train, plane, etc.).
steps: Prepare all documents as PDF files.
Email them to AEMPS at estupefacientes_viajeros@aemps.es at least 10 days before you travel.
The permit is valid for at most 3 months and covers up to 3 months of treatment (15 days for cannabis or its derivatives).

summary: Declare cash or traveller's cheques over USD 10,000. Other monetary instruments must always be declared.

limits.description: Cash or traveller's cheques up to USD 10,000 in total don't need declaring. Monetary instruments other than traveller's cheques must be declared whatever the amount. Money on bank cards isn't declared. Declarations over USD 100,000 need documents showing where the money came from.

notes: Failing to declare goods that must be declared, including monetary instruments, can lead to administrative or criminal penalties under Armenian law.

summary: Up to 10 types of medicine, 3 packs each, for personal use. More if a prescription or doctor's document justifies it.

limits.description: For personal use or treatment, medicines registered or not registered in Armenia can be brought in without certification: up to 10 types, with three consumer packs each, unless a prescription, medical history or other document signed by a doctor justifies a larger quantity for the course of treatment.

notes: Medicine containing narcotic or psychotropic substances follows separate rules (see Armenia's controlled-medication entry).

summary: No licence needed, but only medicines registered in Armenia, with medical documents translated into Armenian and notarised. Declare them.

limits.description: Narcotic and psychotropic medicines can be brought in without a licence if you show medical documents confirming the medical need, with the product name and quantity. The documents, or certified Armenian translations with notarisation, must be given to customs. Only narcotic and psychotropic medicines registered in Armenia may be imported. Fill in a customs declaration stating the quantity prescribed and that it was legally obtained.

notes: Failing to declare medicine containing narcotic or psychotropic substances can lead to administrative or criminal penalties under Armenian law.

The product name and quantity
The originals, or certified translations into Armenian with notarisation

limits.description: Up to 5 kg of pre-packaged animal products without a veterinary sanitary certificate or permission from the exporting country, as long as the factory packaging is intact.

notes: Up to 2 dogs or cats can travel without a special permit if their international passport shows a clinical examination by an authorised body within 14 days before travel.

summary: Up to 6 litres of spirits per traveller, adults only.

limits.description: Only six (6) litres of distilled alcoholic beverages per traveller may be brought in, and only by travellers of legal age.

notes: Goods within the general allowance (USD 500 by air or sea from outside the region, once a year) are duty-free; goods above it are held until a single 50% tax is paid.

limits.description: Only four (4) cartons of cigarettes per traveller may be brought in, and only by travellers of legal age.

summary: Declare cash, precious metals or other monetary instruments over USD 10,000.

limits.description: Carrying cash and securities is legal and untaxed, but anyone carrying cash, precious metals or other monetary instruments over USD 10,000 (or the equivalent) across the border must declare it to customs on the sworn declaration form.

notes: Not declaring leads to a fine set by the Executive Branch, up to the undeclared amount (Law 18.494, Art. 1).

summary: Medicines in quantities that fit your needs and length of stay, over-the-counter or with a prescription.

limits.description: Customs counts as baggage medicines in quantities appropriate to the traveller's needs and length of stay, sold over the counter or, otherwise, with the corresponding prescription.

notes: From customs' baggage page, last updated 19/03/2014. It also lists narcotics (estupefacientes) among goods that may not be brought in.

summary: Fresh fruit and vegetables, seeds, plants, flowers and soil may not be brought in.

limits.description: Customs doesn't allow: plants, their parts and related products; fresh fruit and vegetables; seeds, crafts with seeds and plant products; flowers, ornamental plants and in-vitro cultures; soil, and fruit, vegetable, forage or forest plants or their parts (branches, cuttings, buds, bulbs and similar).

notes: From customs' baggage page, last updated 19/03/2014. Goods subject to specific controls are released only with the agreement of the competent body (such as the agriculture ministry, MGAP).

legal_source.name: Dirección Nacional de Aduanas — Baggage of foreign tourists and returning Uruguayans (last updated 19/03/2014)

summary: Meat, sausages, cheese, butter, cream, eggs and fresh milk may not be brought in. Long-life (UHT) milk is the exception.

limits.description: Customs doesn't allow: fresh milk (long-life milk excepted), butter, eggs, cream and cheese; meat of any species, cold cuts and sausages; domestic animals, birds, exotic species and bees; animal feed and biological or veterinary products.

notes: From customs' baggage page, last updated 19/03/2014.

legal_source.name: Dirección Nacional de Aduanas — Baggage of foreign tourists and returning Uruguayans (last updated 19/03/2014)

summary: Duty-free per traveller per day: 1 litre of spirits over 22% or 2 litres of drinks up to 22%. Not for travellers under 17.

limits.description: Per traveller and per day: 1 litre of alcohol over 22% by volume (or undenatured ethyl alcohol of 80% or more), or 2 litres of drinks of 22% or less, or a proportional mix of the two. Travellers under 17 get no duty-free allowance for alcohol, still wine or beer.

legal_source.name: Indirect Taxation Authority of Bosnia and Herzegovina — Information for citizens and travelers

summary: Duty-free per traveller per day: 200 cigarettes, or 100 cigarillos, or 50 cigars, or 250 g of tobacco. Not for travellers under 17.

limits.description: Per traveller and per day: 200 cigarettes, or 100 cigarillos (cigars of up to 3 g each), or 50 cigars, or 250 g of smoking tobacco, or a proportional mix. Travellers under 17 get no duty-free allowance for tobacco.

legal_source.name: Indirect Taxation Authority of Bosnia and Herzegovina — Information for citizens and travelers

summary: Declare cash, cheques or securities worth more than EUR 10,000 when you enter or leave, on a currency declaration form.

limits.description: Anyone bringing in or taking out cash or securities worth more than EUR 10,000 must declare it to customs at the border crossing, on a currency declaration form available from customs officers or online. This covers foreign currency, convertible marks, cheques, securities and other portable payment instruments. Carrying more than EUR 10,000 in cash also needs approval from the Ministry of Finance of the Republika Srpska or of the Federation of BiH.

legal_source.name: Indirect Taxation Authority of Bosnia and Herzegovina — Information for citizens and travelers

summary: Bring the amount needed for a standard course of treatment, with medical documents such as a prescription or a doctor's note.

limits.description: You can bring medicines for your own use in the quantity needed for a standard therapy, if you carry relevant medical documentation: a medical history transcript, a doctor's permission or a prescription. Medicines you need for personal use don't count towards the 600 BAM duty-free limit on other goods.

summary: Psychotropic medicine: up to 7 days' supply, with medical documents, and declare its name and quantity at the border.

limits.description: Under the Law on the prevention and control of abuse of narcotic drugs, you may carry medicine containing psychotropic substances across the border only with medical documentation and only in the quantity needed for up to 7 days of personal use. People on substitution treatment for addiction, or on symptomatic treatment for terminal cancer, may carry up to 15 days' supply with medical documentation. You must declare the medicine's name and quantity to the customs officer and show the medical documents.

summary: Meat and dairy only from the EU and a few listed European countries. Infant milk, infant food and special medical food: up to 1 kg from anywhere.

limits.description: Personal consignments of meat, milk and their products are allowed only if they come from EU countries, Andorra, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the Faroe Islands, Greenland, Iceland, Montenegro or North Macedonia. Powdered infant milk, infant food and special food needed for medical reasons are allowed up to 1 kg per traveller from any country, if they need no refrigeration before opening, are in branded retail packaging, and the packaging is unopened unless in use. Medical pet food: up to 2 kg from the EU and listed countries (including Serbia), 1 kg from elsewhere, on the same conditions. Products that don't meet these rules must be put in the bins provided on arrival, to be destroyed or taken back.

legal_source.name: Indirect Taxation Authority of Bosnia and Herzegovina — Information for citizens and travelers

summary: Declare cash or bearer negotiable instruments worth MOP 120,000 or more when you arrive. There's no limit on the amount.

limits.description: Travellers bringing into Macao currency or bearer negotiable instruments (such as traveller's cheques, or cheques and promissory notes signed with the payee left blank) worth MOP 120,000 or more, or the equivalent in another currency, must declare them on the customs declaration form. When leaving, you only fill in the form if a customs officer asks. Law 6/2017 sets no limit on the type or amount you can bring in or take out.

notes: A missing, false or incomplete declaration is an administrative offence, fined 1% to 5% of the amount above the threshold, but never less than MOP 1,000 or more than MOP 500,000.

legal_source.name: Macao SAR Customs Service — Declaration for the Transportation of Currency and Bearer Negotiable Instruments (form SA213, general information; Law 6/2017)

summary: Without a medical document: up to 10 different medicines, at most 5 manufacturer's packs of each, for your own use.

limits.description: For personal use during your stay you can bring, without any document from a doctor, up to 10 different medicines and no more than 5 packs of each, plus up to 5 medical devices. Each pack may hold at most: 100 tablets, capsules or similar; 500 g of powder for making a solution; 50 g of homeopathic granules; 500 ml of infusion or oral solution; 10 ampoules or vials of injection; 200 ml or 200 g of a medicine for external use. Medicines must be in the manufacturer's packaging. Since 8 February 2026, customs also take into account the quantity, how often you travel with medicines, and the purpose and length of your trip.

notes: Above these limits you declare the medicines to customs together with a document from a medical institution in your country of residence or stay. That clause was rewritten in 2025 and is published only in Uzbek; LexUz's Russian translation of it is unclear, so check the official text if you need to bring more. Medicines brought in for personal use may not be passed on or sold to anyone else.

legal_source.name: Cabinet of Ministers of Uzbekistan, Resolution No. 191 of 8 June 2016 — Regulation on bringing in and taking out medicines and medical devices by individuals for personal use (as amended to 8 February 2026; LexUz Russian translation of the Uzbek original)

items: Only needed above the limits: a document from a medical institution in your country of residence or stay naming the medicine

summary: Declare narcotic and psychotropic medicines at the border. Narcotics: up to 7 days' supply with a medical document. Psychotropics: up to 5 medicines, 2 packs each.

limits.description: You must declare any narcotic or psychotropic medicines when you cross the border. Narcotic medicines: up to 7 days' supply, with a document from a medical institution in your country of residence or stay giving the medicine's name, its form and the recommended quantity for the course of treatment; show it to customs. Psychotropic medicines: up to 5 different medicines and no more than 2 packs of each, within a course of treatment, without a medical document. Which substances count as narcotic or psychotropic is set by the lists approved by Cabinet Resolution No. 330 of 12 November 2015.

notes: Customs check the documents against what you carry and declare. Any quantity above what the medical document and your declaration show is seized and destroyed.

legal_source.name: Cabinet of Ministers of Uzbekistan, Resolution No. 191 of 8 June 2016 — Regulation on bringing in and taking out medicines and medical devices by individuals for personal use (as amended to 8 February 2026; LexUz Russian translation of the Uzbek original)

items: Issued by a medical institution in your country of residence or stay (required for narcotic medicines)
The medicine's name
Its form (tablets, capsules, solution…)
The recommended quantity for the course of treatment

summary: Duty-free from age 18: 2 litres of drinks up to 16% plus 2 litres over 16%.

limits.description: Passengers aged 18 and over may bring duty-free 2 litres of alcoholic drinks of 16% or less (such as beer, wine and sparkling wine) and 2 litres of drinks over 16% (such as whisky, rum, gin and liqueurs). Duty-free goods must be for your own use. Anything above the allowance must be declared in the red channel and taxed.

notes: Set by the Customs Management (Passenger Allowance) (Amendment) Regulations 2024 (S.I. 94 of 2024). Not declaring goods above the allowance is a serious offence that can bring fines, seizure and prosecution.

legal_source.name: Seychelles Revenue Commission — Customs and Excises (duty-free allowances, cash declaration procedure)

summary: Duty-free from age 18: 200 cigarettes or 250 g of tobacco products.

limits.description: Passengers aged 18 and over may bring duty-free 250 g of tobacco products or 200 cigarettes, the allowance covering cigars, cheroots, snuff and smoking and chewing tobacco. Anything above the allowance must be declared in the red channel and taxed.

notes: Set by the Customs Management (Passenger Allowance) (Amendment) Regulations 2024 (S.I. 94 of 2024). The allowance listed for passengers under 18 covers only SCR 8,000 of other goods, 200 ml of perfume and one electronic item.

legal_source.name: Seychelles Revenue Commission — Customs and Excises (duty-free allowances, cash declaration procedure)

summary: Declare cash worth SCR 50,000 or more (about USD 3,500) when you enter or leave, with proof of where it came from.

limits.description: Anyone carrying cash worth SCR 50,000 or more in total, or the equivalent in foreign currency, must declare it to Customs on entering and on leaving Seychelles. The question also covers monetary instruments such as cheques, bills of exchange, promissory notes, traveller's cheques, bearer bonds and money orders. On arrival, go to the red channel, fill in the Cash Declaration Form and show proof of the source of the funds. On departure, go to the Customs office at the VAT verification counter of the international airport.

notes: Under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism (Cross Border Declaration) Regulations 2022 (S.I. 11 of 2022), failing to declare, or knowingly making a false or misleading declaration, is an offence punishable by a fine on conviction.

legal_source.name: Seychelles Revenue Commission — Customs and Excises (duty-free allowances, cash declaration procedure)

summary: Duty-free: up to 375 ml of spirits and 750 ml of wine. Use the red channel if you carry more.

limits.description: You can bring free of duty portable and perfumed spirits of up to 37.5 centilitres (375 ml) and wine of up to 75 centilitres (750 ml). Drinks above these quantities must go through the red channel and are subject to duties and taxes.

notes: Failing to produce dutiable items for examination makes them liable to forfeiture or a penalty.

legal_source.name: Ghana Revenue Authority — Passengers' Obligations at Customs

summary: Duty-free: cigarettes, cigars and other tobacco up to 0.5 kg (one pound) in total.

limits.description: Cigarettes, cheroots, cigars, tobacco and snuff can be brought in free of duty up to one pound (0.5 kg) in weight in total. Anything above that is subject to duties and taxes and must be declared in the red channel.

notes: Failing to produce dutiable items for examination makes them liable to forfeiture or a penalty.

legal_source.name: Ghana Revenue Authority — Passengers' Obligations at Customs

summary: Duty-free from age 18: 2.5 litres of beer, 2.5 litres of wine and 1.5 litres of spirits.

limits.description: Travellers aged at least 18 may import duty-free 2.5 litres of clear beer, 2.5 litres of wine and 1.5 litres of spirits. The goods must be for your own use, not commercial and not bought for someone else. Anything above the allowance is declared on Form CE6, assessed by Customs and taxed.
limits.quantity: 2.5 L beer + 2.5 L wine + 1.5 L spirits

notes: Separately, travellers may import other goods worth up to USD 1,000 duty-free; gifts for family or friends aren't covered by the rebate.

legal_source.name: Zambia Revenue Authority — Importation of Goods (accompanied baggage: traveller's allowances)

summary: Duty-free from age 18: 400 cigarettes, or 0.5 kg of tobacco, or 0.5 kg of cigars.

limits.description: Travellers aged at least 18 may import duty-free 0.5 kg of tobacco, or 0.5 kg of cigars, or 400 cigarettes. Anything above the allowance is declared on Form CE6, assessed by Customs and taxed.

legal_source.name: Zambia Revenue Authority — Importation of Goods (accompanied baggage: traveller's allowances)

summary: Per person per day, without declaring: 19 cigarettes, or 1 cigar, or 25 g of tobacco.

limits.description: Each day a person may bring in, for their own use and without declaring, 19 cigarettes, or 1 cigar, or 25 g of tobacco, with a total weight of no more than 25 g (the list adds that "the weight of piece must not exceed 3 grams"). Tobacco above that is dutiable and must be declared to Customs on arrival.

notes: The Government Information Bureau announced this lower allowance (19 cigarettes, 1 cigar or 25 g of other tobacco) in a Chief Executive despatch effective 14 July 2015. Failing to declare, or a false declaration, can lead to prosecution and confiscation.

legal_source.name: Civil Aviation Authority Macao — AIP Macao, GEN 1.3 Entry, transit and departure of passengers and crew (customs requirements; current edition, citing Chief Executive Order No. 255/2016, Annex 1)

summary: Per person per day, without declaring: 1 litre of drinks over 30% alcohol.

limits.description: Each day a person may bring in, for their own use and without declaring, 1 litre of drinks with an alcoholic strength over 30% by volume. Dutiable goods above the allowance must be declared to Customs on arrival.

notes: The allowance list covers drinks over 30% only; it doesn't state a quantity for weaker drinks. Commercial goods worth more than MOP 5,000 must always be declared. Failing to declare, or a false declaration, can lead to prosecution and confiscation.

legal_source.name: Civil Aviation Authority Macao — AIP Macao, GEN 1.3 Entry, transit and departure of passengers and crew (customs requirements; current edition, citing Chief Executive Order No. 255/2016, Annex 1)

summary: Declare amounts over USD 5,000 to Customs when you enter or leave, on the Integrated Border Declaration Form.

limits.description: Travellers carrying more than USD 5,000 must declare it before the customs official at the point of entry or exit. The declaration is part of the Integrated Border Declaration Form (on the ZRA Customs Portal or the TaxOnApp mobile app), which can list more than one currency.

legal_source.name: Zambia Revenue Authority — User Guide for the Integrated Border Declaration Form (February 2024), section 6.6 Currency declaration details

summary: Declare more than US$10,000 in full on Form FX-5, with the source and purpose of the funds. Arriving travellers also need proof they declared it where they departed.

limits.description: You can carry up to US$10,000 (or the equivalent in other currencies and monetary instruments) without declaring it. Above that, declare the full amount on the Foreign Currency Declaration Form (FX-5) from the Customs Division of the Ghana Revenue Authority, giving the source and purpose of the funds. Inbound travellers carrying more than US$10,000 must also present proof that they declared it at their port of origin or departure. Outbound travellers with more than US$50,000 must also attach endorsed forex bureau receipts or bank slips showing how the currency was obtained. Monetary instruments include coins, cash, traveller's cheques, personal and cashier's cheques, bearer shares and bonds, money orders, gold, silver, precious stones and prepaid wallets.

notes: Failing to declare, a false declaration, or missing documents can lead to immediate seizure of the undeclared amount, fines or criminal prosecution. Foreign currency may not be sent by mail or cargo; funds sent that way are confiscated. These rules took effect on 1 September 2025.

legal_source.name: Bank of Ghana — Notice No. BG/GOV/SEC/2025/27, Amendment to the Guidelines on the Importation and Exportation of Foreign Currency (August 2025)

summary: Duty-free from age 18: up to 3 L of spirits, or 4.5 L of wine, or 4.5 L of beer.

limits.description: Travellers aged 18 and over may bring duty-free up to 3 litres of spirits, or 4.5 litres of wine, or 4.5 litres of beer, or a combination not exceeding the total limit, as long as it travels with them and isn't for sale or for someone else. Anything over the allowance is subject to duty.

legal_source.name: Fiji Revenue and Customs Service — Arriving in Fiji (last updated 18 September 2025)

summary: Duty-free from age 18: 200 cigarettes or 200 g of cigars or tobacco. Chewing tobacco is prohibited.

limits.description: Travellers aged 18 and over may bring duty-free up to 200 cigarettes, or 200 g of cigars or tobacco, or a combination not exceeding 200 g, as long as it travels with them and isn't for sale or for someone else. Chewing tobacco is prohibited.

legal_source.name: Fiji Revenue and Customs Service — Arriving in Fiji (last updated 18 September 2025)

summary: Duty-free from age 18 within the tobacco allowance: e-cigarettes "up to 200ml/mg", as FRCS puts it.

limits.description: The duty-free tobacco allowance for travellers aged 18 and over lists e-cigarettes "up to 200ml/mg" (the page gives no clearer unit). They must travel with you and not be for sale or for someone else.

legal_source.name: Fiji Revenue and Customs Service — Arriving in Fiji (last updated 18 September 2025)

summary: Declare FJ$10,000 or more (or the foreign-currency equivalent, including negotiable instruments) on a Border Currency Reporting Form.

limits.description: If you carry FJ$10,000 or more, or the equivalent in foreign currency or negotiable instruments, you must declare it and complete a Border Currency Reporting Form.

legal_source.name: Fiji Revenue and Customs Service — Arriving in Fiji (last updated 18 September 2025)

summary: Bring a doctor's prescription for prescription or controlled medicine, for your own use only.

limits.description: If you carry prescription or controlled drugs, bring a doctor's prescription, and make sure the medicine is for your personal use and medically necessary. The page sets no quantity limit.

legal_source.name: Fiji Revenue and Customs Service — Arriving in Fiji (last updated 18 September 2025)

items: A doctor's prescription for each prescription or controlled medicine you carry

source.name: Fiji Revenue and Customs Service — Arriving in Fiji (last updated 18 September 2025)

summary: Declare all food, animal and plant products to the Biosecurity Authority of Fiji, or put them in the amnesty bins.

limits.description: All biosecurity risk goods must be declared to the Biosecurity Authority of Fiji (BAF): food of any kind; animals and animal products such as fish, birds, eggs and honey; plants, fruit, seeds, flowers, wood and soil; used outdoor equipment such as camping gear, sports shoes and tools; and biological specimens. Undeclared items can be dropped in the Biosecurity Amnesty Bins at the border.

notes: Not declaring can bring a FJ$400 spot fine, or prosecution with a fine of up to FJ$20,000, six months' imprisonment, or both.

legal_source.name: Fiji Revenue and Customs Service — Arriving in Fiji (last updated 18 September 2025)

summary: Duty-free from age 18 within the US$200 rebate: up to 5 litres of alcohol, no more than 2 litres of it spirits. Declare it.

limits.description: Under the traveller's partial rebate, travellers aged 18 and over may bring up to 5 litres of alcoholic drinks, of which no more than 2 litres may be spirits, as part of goods worth up to US$200 for personal use. The rebate applies once a month, on your first entry into Zimbabwe in that calendar month, and only if the goods are properly declared and not for resale. Alcohol above 5 litres isn't covered by the rebate and is dutiable.

notes: Crew members of arriving aircraft or vehicles don't get the traveller's rebate.

legal_source.name: Zimbabwe Revenue Authority — Traveller's Rebate

summary: Duty-free from age 18, one option only: 1 L spirits + 2 L wine/beer, or 2 L spirits, or 4 L wine/beer.

limits.description: Passengers aged 18 and over may bring alcohol and tobacco free of duty, excise duty and taxes. Choose ONE option: A) 250 g of tobacco (cigars and cigarettes included), 1 litre of spirits and 2 litres of wine, ale or beer; B) 250 g of tobacco and 2 litres of spirits, no wine or beer; C) 250 g of tobacco and 4 litres of wine, ale or beer, no spirits. Duty, excise duty and VAT are payable on anything above the allowance.

legal_source.name: Mauritius Revenue Authority — Customs: Allowances (alcohol and tobacco table in force from 1 September 2025)

limits.description: Prohibited outright: concealed weapons, catapults and slingshots. Everything else on the police list needs Police Regulatory Department approval before import, and for individuals most of it is 'not allowed' at all: pepper spray, stun and Taser guns, crossbows, flick, butterfly and throwing knives, knuckledusters, nunchaku, ammunition, explosives and fireworks, and toy or replica guns. Swords, spears and daggers can be approved case by case. Real guns are allowed for individuals only for sports shooting at a licensed club, kept at an approved armoury.

notes: Travellers bringing a controlled item must apply for approval at least 2 weeks before travel (processing typically takes 2–3 weeks), declare it to Customs/ICA on arrival and show the approval; items without approval are seized. If you arrive with a prohibited item, declare it to Customs/ICA officers immediately. Importing without approval may lead to seizure, prosecution, fines and/or imprisonment. Toy or replica guns that closely resemble a real gun are not allowed, and personal collection or self-defence don't count as legitimate purposes.
summary: Most weapons need police approval before import, and many aren't allowed for individuals at all: pepper spray, stun guns, flick knives, knuckledusters, replica guns.

legal_source.name: Singapore Police Force, Police Regulatory Department — Guideline on Prohibited, Controlled and Non-Regulated Items (current as of 22 December 2025), Annexes A and B

procedure.title: Get Police Regulatory Department approval before you bring a controlled item
procedure.authority: Police Regulatory Department (PRD), Singapore Police Force
procedure.leadTime: Apply at least 2 weeks before you travel.
steps: Check the item against the guideline's annexes: Annex A items are prohibited and can't be imported at all; Annex B items need PRD approval, and many are not allowed for individuals.

If the item is controlled and allowed for individuals, apply to PRD through its website. Approvals for individuals are case by case, for specific approved activities, and you must show a clear legitimate need.
Travel only after you have PRD's written approval.
On arrival, declare the item to Customs/ICA and show the approval document when asked.
procedure.atTheBorder: Items without approval are seized. If you arrive with a prohibited item, declare it to Customs/ICA officers immediately.

sources.name: Singapore Police Force, Police Regulatory Department — Guideline on Prohibited, Controlled and Non-Regulated Items (current as of 22 December 2025)

limits.description: Bringing firearms, their ammunition or main parts into Türkiye is prohibited, and so are knives and other tools made specially for attack and defence only, such as flick knives and self-defence sprays. The law's exceptions cover only diplomats and certain officials, not ordinary travellers.

notes: Law 6136 Art. 4 names such tools: daggers, switchblades, swords, machetes, bayonets, pointed and grooved knives, maces, garrottes and brass knuckles. It also says the law doesn't govern the use of air guns used only in sport, smoothbore shotguns and their cartridges, or knives that are household items or needed for medicine, industry, farming, sport or a trade. The import ban in Art. 2 is without prejudice to Law 6551 on hunting equipment, whose rules for travellers we haven't checked: ask Turkish customs before travelling with a shotgun.
summary: Banned: firearms, ammunition, and knives made for attack or defence (daggers, switchblades, swords, brass knuckles). Shotguns fall under a separate law.

limits.description: Vietnam restricts medicines it classifies as 'addictive' or 'psychotropic', which include medicines used to treat addiction, anxiety, depression, insomnia and other conditions. It is illegal to have more than 7 days of such medicine prescribed by a doctor. Carry the prescription with the medicine, and a letter from your doctor stating how much you need during your trip.

notes: If you're unsure whether your medicine falls into these categories, or you need to bring more than usually allowed, ask a Vietnamese embassy before travelling. Unofficial summaries of Vietnam's Decree 163/2025/ND-CP give 7 days for addictive medicines and 10 days for psychotropic and precursor medicines (more needs an import permit); the decree text itself couldn't be read here, so this row uses the UK government's single 7-day figure.
summary: Up to 7 days' supply of addictive or psychotropic medicine (e.g. for anxiety, depression, insomnia), with the prescription and a doctor's letter.

How much of the medicine you need during your trip
The doctor's signature and address
